name: Close-Grip Barbell Bench Press
instructions: Lie flat on the bench with a grip just inside shoulder-width.
Unrack the bar and lower it to your lower chest, keeping the elbows tucked close to your body.
Press the bar back up to full arm extension.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
coachNote: The best compound mass-builder for the triceps — keep the elbows tracking close to the torso instead of flaring out.
tips: Keep the wrists stacked directly over the elbows.
Lower the bar to the lower chest, not the neck.
commonMistakes: Gripping too narrow, which can strain the wrists.
Flaring the elbows out wide like a standard bench press.
benefits: Allows heavier loading than isolation triceps work.
Builds pressing strength alongside triceps mass.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter for heavy sets.
Avoid an excessively narrow grip that strains the wrists.
startingPosition: Lying on the bench, arms extended, grip just inside shoulder-width.
endingPosition: Bar lowered to the lower chest, elbows tucked.

name: Close-Grip Dumbbell Bench Press
instructions: Lie on a flat bench holding dumbbells together above the chest, palms facing each other.
Lower the dumbbells while keeping them close together and elbows tucked.
Press back up to full extension, keeping the dumbbells close throughout.
coachNote: Pressing the dumbbells together throughout the set keeps constant inward pressure that increases triceps activation.
tips: Keep the dumbbells pressed together for the whole set.
Keep elbows tucked, not flared.
commonMistakes: Letting the dumbbells drift apart during the press.
Flaring the elbows out to the sides.
benefits: Greater range of motion than a barbell version.
Adjustable hand position for comfort.
safetyNotes: Use a weight you can control through the full range.
Get the dumbbells into position carefully using your knees.
startingPosition: Dumbbells held together above the chest, elbows bent.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended above the chest, dumbbells together.

name: Close-Grip EZ Bar Floor Press
instructions: Lie on the floor with knees bent, holding an EZ bar above the chest with a close grip.
Lower the bar until the upper arms touch the floor.
Press back up to full extension, keeping the elbows tucked.
coachNote: The floor limits the range of motion at the bottom, emphasizing lockout strength while reducing shoulder strain.
tips: Pause briefly when the upper arms touch the floor.
Keep the wrists stacked over the elbows.
commonMistakes: Bouncing the elbows off the floor.
Flaring the elbows out during the press.
benefits: Reduces shoulder strain by limiting range of motion.
Builds strong lockout strength for pressing.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter or safety setup for heavier loads.
Keep the descent controlled.
startingPosition: Lying on the floor, bar held above the chest, knees bent.
endingPosition: Bar lowered until upper arms touch the floor.

name: Barbell Skull Crusher
instructions: Lie flat on a bench holding a barbell above your chest with a close grip, arms extended.
Bend the elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead, keeping the upper arms still.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: Keep the upper arms perpendicular to the floor throughout — all the movement should come from the elbow hinge.
tips: Lower the bar toward the forehead or just behind the head, not straight down onto the face.
Keep the elbows pointed toward the ceiling, not flared out.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drift outward during the lowering phase.
Moving the upper arms instead of just hinging at the elbow.
benefits: Strong stretch and isolation for all three triceps heads.
Effective mass builder when performed with control.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter or lighter weight since the bar passes close to the face.
Consider an EZ bar if wrist discomfort occurs.
startingPosition: Arms extended above the chest, bar held with a close grip.
endingPosition: Bar lowered toward the forehead, elbows bent.

name: EZ Bar Skull Crusher
instructions: Lie flat on a bench holding an EZ bar above your chest with arms extended.
Bend the elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead, keeping the upper arms still.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: The angled EZ bar grip is easier on the wrists than a straight bar for this exercise.
tips: Keep the upper arms fixed and perpendicular to the floor.
Control the descent, don't let the bar drop quickly.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Moving the shoulders to help lower the bar.
benefits: Wrist-friendly alternative to a straight barbell skull crusher.
Strong triceps stretch and contraction.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter for heavier loads.
Control the bar path carefully near the face.
startingPosition: Arms extended above the chest, EZ bar in hand.
endingPosition: Bar lowered toward the forehead, elbows bent.

name: Reverse-Grip EZ Bar Skull Crusher
instructions: Lie flat on a bench holding an EZ bar above your chest with an underhand grip.
Bend the elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: The underhand grip changes the resistance curve and can increase activation of the long head of the triceps for some lifters.
tips: Use a lighter weight than the standard grip version.
Keep the elbows fixed and pointed at the ceiling.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight before adapting to the unfamiliar grip.
Letting the elbows flare outward.
benefits: Unique resistance curve for triceps development.
Adds variety for lifters chasing new stimulus.
safetyNotes: Start light to adapt to the underhand grip.
Use a spotter for heavier attempts.
startingPosition: Arms extended above the chest, underhand grip on the EZ bar.
endingPosition: Bar lowered toward the forehead, elbows bent.

name: Dumbbell Skull Crusher
instructions: Lie flat on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand above your chest, palms facing each other.
Bend the elbows to lower the dumbbells toward your head, keeping the upper arms still.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: Dumbbells allow a more natural wrist path and independent arm control compared to a fixed bar.
tips: Keep the upper arms fixed throughout the movement.
Lower the dumbbells alongside your head, not directly onto it.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Using too much weight and losing control near the head.
benefits: Independent arm control reduces imbalances.
Strong stretch and isolation for the triceps.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo, especially lowering near the head.
Start with lighter dumbbells than your bar skull crusher.
startingPosition: Arms extended above the chest, dumbbells in hand.
endingPosition: Dumbbells lowered toward the head, elbows bent.

name: Incline EZ Bar Skull Crusher
instructions: Lie back on an incline bench holding an EZ bar above your chest with arms extended.
Bend the elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: The incline angle shifts more emphasis onto the long head of the triceps compared to a flat bench version.
tips: Keep the upper arms fixed throughout.
Control the descent carefully.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Using a bench angle too steep, turning it into an overhead extension.
benefits: Emphasizes the long head of the triceps.
Adds variety to standard flat skull crushers.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter for heavier loads.
Control the bar path near the face.
startingPosition: Seated on incline bench, arms extended above the chest.
endingPosition: Bar lowered toward the forehead, elbows bent.

name: Cable Skull Crusher (Rope, Lying)
instructions: Lie on a bench positioned so a low cable pulley is behind your head, holding a rope attachment above your chest.
Bend the elbows to lower the rope toward your forehead.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: The cable keeps constant tension throughout, unlike a free-weight skull crusher which loses tension near lockout.
tips: Keep the upper arms fixed throughout.
Separate the rope ends slightly at the bottom for extra contraction.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Using too much weight and losing control of the rope.
benefits: Constant tension throughout the full range of motion.
Reduces the risk of dropping a free weight near the face.
safetyNotes: Position the bench securely relative to the cable pulley.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Arms extended above the chest, rope in hand.
endingPosition: Rope lowered toward the forehead, elbows bent.

name: JM Press
instructions: Lie on a flat bench holding a barbell above your chest with a close grip.
Lower the bar in a hybrid path between a skull crusher and a close-grip press, bringing it toward your upper chest/chin.
Press the bar back up to full extension, driving through the triceps.
coachNote: This hybrid movement allows heavier loading than a strict skull crusher while still emphasizing the triceps more than a standard close-grip press.
tips: Find a bar path that feels like a blend between the two movements.
Keep the elbows pointed forward, not flared.
commonMistakes: Turning it into a pure skull crusher or pure press instead of the hybrid path.
Using too much weight before mastering the technique.
benefits: Allows heavier loading than isolation triceps work.
Popular among powerlifters for building pressing lockout strength.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter for heavier sets.
Master the standard close-grip press and skull crusher first.
startingPosition: Arms extended above the chest, close grip on the bar.
endingPosition: Bar lowered to the upper chest/chin area, elbows bent.

name: Tate Press
instructions: Lie flat on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand above your chest, elbows flared out to the sides.
Lower the dumbbells by bending the elbows, bringing them toward your chest with the elbows pointing outward.
Press the dumbbells back up to the starting position by extending the elbows.
coachNote: The flared elbow position is intentional here — this changes the tension curve compared to a standard skull crusher.
tips: Keep the dumbbells' path controlled and consistent.
Focus on driving through the triceps to press back up.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight and losing control near the chest.
Turning it into a standard dumbbell press.
benefits: Unique elbow-out angle for triceps development.
Adds variety to standard skull crusher training.
safetyNotes: Use a lighter weight than a standard skull crusher to learn the pattern.
Keep the movement controlled throughout.
startingPosition: Arms extended above the chest, elbows flared, dumbbells in hand.
endingPosition: Dumbbells lowered toward the chest, elbows bent and flared.

name: California Press
instructions: Lie flat on a bench holding a barbell above your chest with a close-to-medium grip.
Lower the bar toward your neck/upper chest with the elbows tucked close, similar to a skull crusher angle.
Press the bar back up to full extension, similar to a close-grip bench press.
coachNote: This blends a skull crusher's stretch with a close-grip press's lockout strength for a well-rounded triceps stimulus.
tips: Keep the elbows tucked throughout the entire rep.
Control the descent toward the neck/upper chest carefully.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare out during the press.
Using too much weight before mastering the bar path.
benefits: Combines a stretch position with strong lockout training.
Efficient triceps-focused pressing variation.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter for heavier sets.
Keep the bar path controlled near the neck.
startingPosition: Arms extended above the chest, close-medium grip on the bar.
endingPosition: Bar lowered toward the neck/upper chest, elbows tucked.

name: Overhead Dumbbell Triceps Extension (Two-Hand, Seated)
instructions: Sit upright holding a single dumbbell with both hands above your head, arms extended.
Lower the dumbbell behind your head by bending the elbows.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: The overhead position places the long head of the triceps in a deep stretch, which the pushdown variations don't achieve.
tips: Keep the elbows pointed forward and close to the head.
Lower the dumbbell only as far as comfortable shoulder mobility allows.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Arching the lower back to compensate for tight shoulders.
benefits: Deep stretch position for the long head of the triceps.
Simple, minimal equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter or lighter weight when learning.
Keep the core braced to avoid arching the back.
startingPosition: Seated, dumbbell held overhead with both hands, arms extended.
endingPosition: Dumbbell lowered behind the head, elbows bent.

name: Single-Arm Overhead Dumbbell Extension
instructions: Stand or sit holding a dumbbell overhead in one hand, arm fully extended.
Lower the dumbbell behind your head by bending the elbow.
Extend the elbow back to the starting position, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Training one arm at a time allows a deeper stretch and helps correct strength imbalances.
tips: Use the free hand to lightly support the working elbow.
Keep the elbow pointed forward, close to the head.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbow flare outward.
Using too much weight and losing control behind the head.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Deep stretch position for the triceps long head.
safetyNotes: Use a lighter weight than the two-hand version.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Dumbbell held overhead in one hand, arm extended.
endingPosition: Dumbbell lowered behind the head, elbow bent.

name: Overhead EZ Bar Extension (Standing)
instructions: Stand holding an EZ bar overhead with both hands, arms fully extended.
Lower the bar behind your head by bending the elbows.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: Standing removes back support, requiring more core bracing than the seated version.
tips: Keep the elbows pointed forward throughout.
Brace the core to avoid arching the lower back.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Using momentum from the hips to move the weight.
benefits: Deep stretch position for the triceps long head.
Builds core stability alongside triceps strength.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter or lighter weight when learning.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, EZ bar held overhead, arms extended.
endingPosition: Bar lowered behind the head, elbows bent.

name: Seated Overhead Barbell Extension
instructions: Sit upright on a bench holding a barbell overhead with a close grip, arms extended.
Lower the bar behind your head by bending the elbows.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: Also known as the French press — the seated back support removes momentum for a stricter contraction.
tips: Keep the elbows pointed forward throughout.
Lower only as far as your shoulder mobility comfortably allows.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Arching the back to compensate for tight shoulders.
benefits: Removes momentum for a stricter isolation.
Deep stretch for the long head of the triceps.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter or lighter weight when learning.
Keep the back flat against the bench pad.
startingPosition: Seated, bar held overhead, arms extended.
endingPosition: Bar lowered behind the head, elbows bent.

name: Overhead Cable Triceps Extension (Rope, Standing)
instructions: Stand facing away from a low cable pulley, holding a rope attachment overhead with both hands.
Lower the rope behind your head by bending the elbows.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: Cables keep constant tension on the long head of the triceps throughout the entire stretched range.
tips: Keep the elbows pointed forward and relatively fixed.
Step forward enough to keep tension on the cable throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Using the shoulders to help move the weight.
benefits: Constant tension through the deepest stretch position.
Easy to adjust load in small increments.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Standing, rope held overhead, arms extended.
endingPosition: Rope lowered behind the head, elbows bent.

name: Seated Overhead Cable Extension (Rope)
instructions: Sit on a bench positioned in front of a low cable pulley, holding a rope attachment overhead.
Lower the rope behind your head by bending the elbows.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: The seated position removes leg drive, isolating the triceps more strictly than the standing version.
tips: Keep the elbows pointed forward throughout.
Sit tall and avoid leaning excessively forward or back.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Using body momentum to move the weight.
benefits: Removes lower-body momentum for stricter isolation.
Constant cable tension through the stretch.
safetyNotes: Position the bench securely relative to the cable pulley.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Seated, rope held overhead, arms extended.
endingPosition: Rope lowered behind the head, elbows bent.

name: Single-Arm Overhead Cable Extension
instructions: Stand facing away from a low cable pulley, holding a single handle overhead in one hand.
Lower the handle behind your head by bending the elbow.
Extend the elbow back to the starting position, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Training one arm at a time allows a stronger mind-muscle connection and helps correct imbalances.
tips: Keep the elbow pointed forward and relatively fixed.
Brace the core to avoid twisting the torso.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbow flare outward.
Rotating the torso to assist the movement.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Constant tension through the deepest stretch position.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Standing, handle held overhead in one hand, arm extended.
endingPosition: Handle lowered behind the head, elbow bent.

name: Cable Triceps Pushdown (Straight Bar)
instructions: Stand facing a high cable pulley holding a straight bar attachment with an overhand grip.
Keeping the elbows pinned to your sides, push the bar down until arms are fully extended.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The classic triceps isolation staple — keep the elbows completely still throughout, letting only the forearm move.
tips: Keep the elbows glued to your sides throughout.
Avoid leaning forward to help push the weight down.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drift away from the body.
Using the shoulders and torso to help push the bar down.
benefits: Simple, effective triceps isolation.
Easy to progressively overload.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, upright stance.
Use a controlled tempo, avoid locking out aggressively.
startingPosition: Elbows bent at the sides, bar at chest height.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended down, bar at the thighs.

name: Cable Triceps Pushdown (Rope)
instructions: Stand facing a high cable pulley holding a rope attachment with a neutral grip.
Keeping the elbows pinned to your sides, push the rope down until arms are fully extended, separating the rope ends at the bottom.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The rope's free movement allows a stronger peak contraction than a fixed bar by separating the hands at the bottom.
tips: Separate the rope ends outward at the bottom for extra contraction.
Keep the elbows glued to your sides.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drift away from the body.
Skipping the rope separation at the bottom.
benefits: Allows a stronger peak contraction than a straight bar.
Constant cable tension throughout the range.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, upright stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Elbows bent at the sides, rope at chest height.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended down, rope ends separated.

name: Cable Triceps Pushdown (V-Bar)
instructions: Stand facing a high cable pulley holding a V-bar attachment with a neutral grip.
Keeping the elbows pinned to your sides, push the bar down until arms are fully extended.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The angled V-bar grip is often more comfortable on the wrists than a straight bar for pushdowns.
tips: Keep the elbows glued to your sides.
Avoid leaning forward to help push the weight down.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drift away from the body.
Using the shoulders to help push the bar down.
benefits: Wrist-friendly grip alternative.
Simple, effective triceps isolation.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, upright stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Elbows bent at the sides, V-bar at chest height.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended down.

name: Reverse-Grip Cable Pushdown
instructions: Stand facing a high cable pulley holding a straight bar with an underhand grip.
Keeping the elbows pinned to your sides, push the bar down until arms are fully extended.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The underhand grip shifts more emphasis onto the inner head of the triceps compared to a standard overhand pushdown.
tips: Keep the elbows glued to your sides.
Use a lighter weight than a standard pushdown to start.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drift away from the body.
Using too much weight before adapting to the grip.
benefits: Emphasizes the inner head of the triceps.
Adds variety to standard pushdown training.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, upright stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Elbows bent at the sides, underhand grip on the bar.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended down.

name: Single-Arm Cable Pushdown
instructions: Stand facing a high cable pulley holding a single handle with an overhand grip.
Keeping the elbow pinned to your side, push the handle down until the arm is fully extended.
Return with control, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Training one arm at a time allows a stronger mind-muscle connection and helps correct imbalances.
tips: Keep the elbow glued to your side throughout.
Avoid rotating the torso to assist the push.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbow drift away from the body.
Using the torso to help push the weight down.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Allows a fuller stretch and contraction than bilateral pushdowns.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Elbow bent at the side, handle at chest height.
endingPosition: Arm fully extended down.

name: Single-Arm Reverse-Grip Cable Pushdown
instructions: Stand facing a high cable pulley holding a single handle with an underhand grip.
Keeping the elbow pinned to your side, push the handle down until the arm is fully extended.
Return with control, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Combining the underhand grip with unilateral training gives a strong peak contraction and inner-head emphasis.
tips: Keep the elbow glued to your side throughout.
Rotate the wrist slightly at the bottom for extra contraction.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbow drift away from the body.
Using the torso to help push the weight down.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Emphasizes the inner head of the triceps.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Elbow bent at the side, underhand grip on the handle.
endingPosition: Arm fully extended down.

name: Machine Triceps Pushdown
instructions: Sit or stand at the machine gripping the handles with elbows at your sides.
Push the handles down until arms are fully extended.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A stable, guided option for beginners or for training close to failure without needing a cable stack setup.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
Focus on a slow, controlled tempo.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drift away from the body.
Using too much weight and losing strict form.
benefits: Guided path reduces stabilizer demand.
Easy to progressively overload with the weight stack.
safetyNotes: Adjust seat/handle position correctly before loading.
Avoid locking out aggressively at the bottom.
startingPosition: Elbows bent at the sides, handles at chest height.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended down.

name: Machine Triceps Extension
instructions: Sit in the machine with your upper arms resting against the pad, gripping the handles.
Extend your arms by pushing the handles forward or down, depending on the machine design.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A beginner-friendly isolation option since the machine controls the movement path for you.
tips: Keep the upper arms fixed against the pad throughout.
Focus on a slow, controlled tempo.
commonMistakes: Lifting the upper arms off the pad.
Using too much weight and losing strict form.
benefits: Very beginner-friendly with a fixed, safe path.
Good triceps isolation without stabilizer demand.
safetyNotes: Adjust seat and pad position correctly before loading.
Avoid locking out aggressively.
startingPosition: Upper arms on the pad, elbows bent.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended.

name: Dumbbell Kickback
instructions: Place one knee and hand on a bench for support, holding a dumbbell in the opposite hand with the upper arm parallel to the floor.
Extend the elbow to straighten the arm behind you.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Keep the upper arm perfectly still and parallel to the floor throughout — the movement should come only from the elbow.
tips: Keep the upper arm fixed and parallel to the torso.
Squeeze the triceps hard at full extension.
commonMistakes: Swinging the upper arm to help move the weight.
Using too much weight, which limits the range of motion.
benefits: Strong peak contraction at full extension.
Simple, minimal equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Use a light-to-moderate weight since strict form is essential.
Keep a stable base with the supporting knee and hand.
startingPosition: Upper arm parallel to the floor, elbow bent, dumbbell held.
endingPosition: Arm fully extended straight behind the body.

name: Cable Kickback
instructions: Stand facing a low cable pulley, hinged forward with the upper arm parallel to the floor, holding a handle.
Extend the elbow to straighten the arm behind you.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Cables keep constant tension throughout, unlike a dumbbell kickback which loses tension at the top.
tips: Keep the upper arm fixed and parallel to the torso.
Squeeze the triceps hard at full extension.
commonMistakes: Swinging the upper arm to help move the weight.
Standing too upright, reducing the range of motion.
benefits: Constant tension throughout the full range of motion.
Strong peak contraction at full extension.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, hinged stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Upper arm parallel to the floor, elbow bent, handle held.
endingPosition: Arm fully extended straight behind the body.

name: Resistance Band Kickback
instructions: Anchor a resistance band under your foot or a low point, hinge forward holding the band with the upper arm parallel to the floor.
Extend the elbow to straighten the arm behind you.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A convenient triceps option for home or travel training when no dumbbells or cables are available.
tips: Keep the upper arm fixed and parallel to the torso.
Squeeze the triceps at full extension.
commonMistakes: Swinging the upper arm to help move the band.
Using a band too heavy to control with strict form.
benefits: Portable, minimal equipment needed.
Constant tension throughout the range of motion.
safetyNotes: Check the band for wear before use.
Keep a stable, hinged stance.
startingPosition: Upper arm parallel to the floor, elbow bent, band held.
endingPosition: Arm fully extended straight behind the body.

name: Bench Dip
instructions: Sit on the edge of a bench with hands gripping the edge beside your hips, legs extended in front of you.
Lower your body by bending the elbows until they reach roughly 90 degrees.
Press back up to the starting position by extending the elbows.
coachNote: Keep the torso close to the bench and elbows pointed backward, not flared, to protect the shoulders.
tips: Keep the hips close to the bench throughout the movement.
Keep the elbows pointed straight back.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips drift too far from the bench, straining the shoulders.
Going too low, causing shoulder impingement.
benefits: No equipment needed beyond a bench.
Simple bodyweight triceps builder.
safetyNotes: Avoid excessive depth if you feel shoulder discomfort.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Hands on the bench edge, legs extended, hips near the bench.
endingPosition: Elbows bent to roughly 90 degrees, hips lowered.

name: Weighted Bench Dip
instructions: Set up as in a standard bench dip with a weight plate resting on your thighs.
Lower your body by bending the elbows until they reach roughly 90 degrees.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: Only progress to added weight once bodyweight bench dips are easy for high reps.
tips: Have the plate balanced securely on the thighs before starting.
Keep the elbows pointed straight back.
commonMistakes: Adding too much weight too soon, breaking form.
Going too low and straining the shoulders.
benefits: Allows progressive overload on a bodyweight movement.
Builds significant triceps strength.
safetyNotes: Have a partner assist with plate placement if needed.
Start with light added weight.
startingPosition: Hands on the bench edge, plate on thighs, hips near the bench.
endingPosition: Elbows bent to roughly 90 degrees, hips lowered.

name: Triceps Dip (Parallel Bars)
instructions: Grip the dip bars and lift yourself up with arms extended, torso upright.
Lower your body by bending the elbows, keeping the torso as vertical as possible.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: Staying upright shifts the emphasis toward the triceps, while leaning forward shifts it toward the chest.
tips: Keep the torso as upright as possible throughout.
Control the descent rather than dropping.
commonMistakes: Leaning forward too much, turning it into a chest-dominant movement.
Going too deep and straining the shoulder joint.
benefits: Strong compound triceps builder.
Can be loaded with a weight belt as strength increases.
safetyNotes: Avoid excessive depth if you feel shoulder strain.
Build up shoulder mobility before adding weight.
startingPosition: Arms extended, torso upright, supporting body weight on the bars.
endingPosition: Elbows bent, body lowered with an upright torso.

name: Weighted Triceps Dip
instructions: Attach a weight belt or hold a dumbbell between your feet, then grip the dip bars with an upright torso.
Lower your body by bending the elbows.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: Only progress to added weight once bodyweight dips are easy for 12-15 controlled reps.
tips: Keep the torso upright to maintain triceps emphasis.
Add weight gradually as strength improves.
commonMistakes: Adding too much weight too soon, breaking form.
Leaning forward excessively, shifting emphasis to the chest.
benefits: Allows significant progressive overload on a bodyweight movement.
Builds serious triceps and pressing strength.
safetyNotes: Use a secure weight belt or dumbbell attachment.
Build up shoulder mobility before adding weight.
startingPosition: Arms extended, torso upright, weight attached, supporting body weight on the bars.
endingPosition: Elbows bent, body lowered with an upright torso.

name: Machine Assisted Triceps Dip
instructions: Kneel or stand on the assisted dip machine platform, gripping the parallel handles with an upright torso.
Lower your body by bending the elbows.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: Reduce the assistance weight over time as you get stronger, working toward an unassisted dip.
tips: Choose an assistance level that allows 6-10 controlled reps.
Keep the torso upright to emphasize the triceps.
commonMistakes: Using too much assistance for too long, slowing progress.
Leaning forward, shifting emphasis to the chest.
benefits: Lets beginners build toward a full dip safely.
Adjustable difficulty via the assistance stack.
safetyNotes: Step onto and off the platform carefully.
Choose a stable, controlled assistance level.
startingPosition: Kneeling on platform, arms extended, torso upright.
endingPosition: Elbows bent, body lowered.

name: Close-Grip Push-Up
instructions: Start in a plank position with hands roughly shoulder-width apart or slightly closer.
Lower your body while keeping the elbows tracking close to your sides.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: A slightly narrower hand position than a standard push-up shifts more emphasis onto the triceps without the wrist strain of a diamond push-up.
tips: Keep the elbows tucked close to the body throughout.
Keep the body in a straight line from head to heels.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag or pike up.
Flaring the elbows out to the sides.
benefits: No equipment needed.
Builds functional triceps and pressing strength.
safetyNotes: Scale to an incline version if full range is too difficult.
Keep the neck neutral throughout.
startingPosition: Plank position, hands roughly shoulder-width, arms extended.
endingPosition: Chest close to the floor, elbows bent and tucked.

name: Decline Close-Grip Push-Up
instructions: Place your feet on an elevated surface and hands close together on the floor.
Lower your body while keeping the elbows tucked close to your sides.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: Elevating the feet increases the load on the triceps and shoulders compared to a standard close-grip push-up.
tips: Keep core tight to avoid hip sag with the added leverage.
Keep the elbows tucked throughout.
commonMistakes: Feet placed too high before building enough strength.
Losing the straight body line under increased load.
benefits: Increases difficulty without needing added weight.
Strong triceps and shoulder builder.
safetyNotes: Choose a stable elevated surface.
Progress the foot height gradually.
startingPosition: Feet elevated, hands close together on the floor.
endingPosition: Chest close to the floor, elbows bent and tucked.

name: TRX Triceps Extension
instructions: Hold the TRX handles and face away from the anchor point, leaning forward with arms extended overhead.
Bend the elbows to lower your body toward your hands, keeping the upper arms fixed.
Extend the elbows to press back to the starting position.
coachNote: Difficulty is adjusted by changing your body angle — more upright is easier, more horizontal is harder.
tips: Keep the upper arms fixed near your head throughout.
Keep the body rigid like a plank.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Using a body angle too difficult for current strength level.
benefits: Highly scalable difficulty via body angle.
Portable, minimal equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Ensure the TRX anchor point is secure before use.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Leaning forward, arms extended overhead, body straight.
endingPosition: Body lowered toward the hands, elbows bent.

name: TRX Triceps Press
instructions: Hold the TRX handles and lean forward with arms extended, body in a straight line, hands close together.
Lower your body by bending the elbows close to your sides, similar to a close-grip push-up.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: The unstable handles add a stabilization challenge on top of the standard triceps press pattern.
tips: Keep the elbows tucked close to the body.
Keep the body rigid like a plank throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Letting the hips sag.
benefits: Adds an instability and core-stability component to a triceps press.
Portable, minimal equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Ensure the TRX anchor point is secure before use.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Leaning forward, arms extended, body straight, hands close together.
endingPosition: Body lowered, elbows bent and tucked.

name: Plate Overhead Triceps Extension
instructions: Stand or sit holding a weight plate overhead with both hands, arms extended.
Lower the plate behind your head by bending the elbows.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: A simple accessible option when barbells or dumbbells aren't available for overhead extension work.
tips: Grip the plate securely at the edges.
Keep the elbows pointed forward throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Gripping the plate too loosely, causing it to shift.
benefits: Adds a grip-strength component to an overhead extension.
Minimal equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Use a plate weight you can control comfortably.
Keep the core braced to avoid arching the back.
startingPosition: Plate held overhead with both hands, arms extended.
endingPosition: Plate lowered behind the head, elbows bent.

name: Landmine Triceps Extension
instructions: Kneel or stand holding the sleeve end of a landmine-anchored barbell close to your shoulder, upper arm fixed.
Extend the elbow to press the sleeve forward and up.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The fixed pivot point creates a unique resistance curve compared to a free dumbbell or cable extension.
tips: Keep the upper arm fixed throughout the movement.
Brace the core to avoid excessive torso rotation.
commonMistakes: Using the shoulder to help press the weight.
Standing too far from the pivot, limiting range of motion.
benefits: Unique resistance curve for triceps development.
Minimal equipment needed beyond a barbell and anchor.
safetyNotes: Secure the barbell end firmly in the landmine attachment.
Start light to learn the movement path.
startingPosition: Sleeve held near the shoulder, elbow bent, upper arm fixed.
endingPosition: Arm extended forward and up.

name: Smith Machine Close-Grip Bench Press
instructions: Position a bench under the Smith machine bar and lie back with a close grip on the bar.
Unrack the bar and lower it to your lower chest, keeping the elbows tucked.
Press back up to full extension.
coachNote: The fixed bar path allows safe training near failure without a spotter.
tips: Position the bench so the bar path lines up over the lower chest.
Keep the elbows tucked throughout.
commonMistakes: Bench misaligned with the bar path.
Flaring the elbows out to the sides.
benefits: Allows safe near-failure training.
Fixed path reduces stabilization demand.
safetyNotes: Confirm the safety hooks are set correctly.
Double check the bar is locked before releasing.
startingPosition: Bar racked above the chest, close grip.
endingPosition: Bar lowered to the lower chest, elbows tucked.

name: Resistance Band Pushdown
instructions: Anchor a resistance band overhead or at a high point, holding the ends with elbows bent at your sides.
Push the band down until arms are fully extended.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A convenient triceps option for home or travel training when no cable machine is available.
tips: Keep the elbows glued to your sides.
Use a band with enough tension to challenge the triceps through the full range.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drift away from the body.
Using a band too heavy to control with strict form.
benefits: Portable, minimal equipment needed.
Constant tension throughout the range of motion.
safetyNotes: Check the band for wear before use.
Ensure the anchor point is secure and high enough.
startingPosition: Elbows bent at the sides, band anchored overhead.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended down.

name: Resistance Band Overhead Extension
instructions: Stand on one end of a resistance band, holding the other end overhead with both hands, arms extended.
Lower the band behind your head by bending the elbows.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: A convenient overhead extension option for home or travel training when no dumbbells or cables are available.
tips: Keep the elbows pointed forward throughout.
Brace the core to avoid arching the back.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Using a band too heavy to control near the head.
benefits: Portable, minimal equipment needed.
Deep stretch position for the long head of the triceps.
safetyNotes: Check the band for wear before use.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing on the band, band held overhead, arms extended.
endingPosition: Band lowered behind the head, elbows bent.

name: Lying Cable Extension (Pullover-Style)
instructions: Lie on a bench with your head near a low cable pulley, holding a straight bar or rope overhead with arms extended.
Bend the elbows to lower the attachment behind your head.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position, pressing the attachment up and over your chest.
coachNote: The unique cable angle here keeps tension on the triceps through both the stretch and the lockout, similar to a pullover pattern.
tips: Keep the upper arms relatively fixed throughout.
Control the tempo, especially through the stretch position.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Using the shoulders to help move the weight.
benefits: Unique cable angle for continuous triceps tension.
Combines a stretch and lockout in one movement.
safetyNotes: Position the bench securely relative to the cable pulley.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Lying on the bench, arms extended overhead toward the low pulley.
endingPosition: Attachment lowered behind the head, elbows bent.

name: Rolling Dumbbell Triceps Extension
instructions: Lie flat on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand above your chest, arms extended.
Lower the dumbbells by rolling the upper arms back so the dumbbells travel behind your head in an arc.
Reverse the motion, pressing the dumbbells back up and forward to the starting position.
coachNote: Allowing the upper arms to roll back (unlike a strict skull crusher) increases the stretch on the long head of the triceps.
tips: Keep the movement smooth and controlled through the entire arc.
Use a lighter weight than a standard skull crusher.
commonMistakes: Moving too quickly through the stretch position.
Using too much weight and losing control behind the head.
benefits: Increases the stretch on the long head of the triceps.
Unique variation to break through hypertrophy plateaus.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter or lighter weight when learning.
Control the bar path carefully near the head.
startingPosition: Arms extended above the chest, dumbbells in hand.
endingPosition: Dumbbells lowered behind the head via a rolling arc, elbows bent.

name: Cross-Body Cable Extension (Single-Arm)
instructions: Stand sideways to a high cable pulley, holding a handle with the far hand across your body.
Extend the elbow to pull the handle down and across toward your opposite hip.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The cross-body angle provides a unique resistance curve compared to a standard pushdown, hitting the triceps from a different line of pull.
tips: Keep the elbow relatively fixed as you extend.
Avoid using the torso to help pull the weight down.
commonMistakes: Rotating the torso excessively to assist the movement.
Using too much weight and losing control of the path.
benefits: Unique angle for triceps development.
Constant cable tension throughout the range.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Handle held across the body at shoulder height, elbow bent.
endingPosition: Arm extended down and across toward the opposite hip.

name: Kneeling Cable Rope Overhead Extension
instructions: Kneel facing away from a low cable pulley, holding a rope attachment overhead with both hands.
Lower the rope behind your head by bending the elbows.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: The kneeling position removes leg drive and adds a core-stability demand compared to the standing version.
tips: Keep the elbows pointed forward throughout.
Brace the core to maintain an upright kneeling posture.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Leaning too far forward or back during the set.
benefits: Removes lower-body momentum for stricter isolation.
Adds a core stability component to the extension.
safetyNotes: Use a stable kneeling surface or pad.
Keep a controlled tempo throughout.
startingPosition: Kneeling, rope held overhead, arms extended.
endingPosition: Rope lowered behind the head, elbows bent.

name: Dumbbell Floor Press (Close-Grip)
instructions: Lie on the floor with knees bent, holding a dumbbell in each hand above your chest, close together.
Lower the dumbbells until your upper arms touch the floor.
Press back up to full extension, keeping the dumbbells close throughout.
coachNote: The floor limits range of motion at the bottom, emphasizing lockout strength while reducing shoulder strain.
tips: Pause briefly when the upper arms touch the floor.
Keep the dumbbells close together throughout the press.
commonMistakes: Bouncing the elbows off the floor.
Letting the dumbbells drift apart.
benefits: Reduces shoulder strain by limiting range of motion.
Builds strong lockout strength for the triceps.
safetyNotes: Use a weight you can control through the full range.
Keep the descent controlled to protect the elbows.
startingPosition: Lying on the floor, dumbbells held above the chest, knees bent.
endingPosition: Dumbbells lowered until upper arms touch the floor.

name: Incline Cable Triceps Extension
instructions: Lie back on an incline bench positioned in front of a low cable pulley, holding a rope attachment overhead.
Lower the rope behind your head by bending the elbows.
Extend the elbows back to the starting position.
coachNote: The incline angle combined with cable tension emphasizes the long head of the triceps through a deep, constantly-loaded stretch.
tips: Keep the upper arms fixed throughout.
Control the descent carefully.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Using a bench angle too steep, reducing the stretch benefit.
benefits: Emphasizes the long head of the triceps.
Constant tension through the full range of motion.
safetyNotes: Position the bench securely relative to the cable pulley.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Seated on incline bench, rope held overhead, arms extended.
endingPosition: Rope lowered behind the head, elbows bent.
